accepted.label: McCulloch-Pitts neuron model
accepted.description: The first computational model of a neuron proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, representing neurons as simple electrical circuits with binary outputs.
coverage_criteria: Identify McCulloch and Pitts as the authors of the first formal neuron model in 1943.
Describe the basic idea of a simplified neuron with binary output.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate defines the concept.

accepted.label: Hebbian learning
accepted.description: The principle that neural connections are strengthened when the pre- and post-synaptic neurons fire together, introduced by Donald Hebb in 1949 and later formalized as a learning rule.
coverage_criteria: State Hebb's postulate: 'neurons that fire together wire together'.
Give one example of a Hebbian-like learning rule.
accepted.merge_rationale: Both candidates describe the same foundational learning principle; c45 provides the historical introduction and c46 elaborates on variations.

accepted.label: Perceptron
accepted.description: A single-layer neural network model by Frank Rosenblatt (1958) that computes a weighted sum of inputs, subtracts a threshold, and outputs a binary class; it defines a linear decision boundary.
coverage_criteria: Explain the perceptron architecture: inputs, weights, bias, activation (step function).
State that the perceptron performs binary classification and can learn simple linearly separable patterns.
accepted.merge_rationale: All three candidates describe the perceptron, either historically (c45, c50) or architecturally (c46); together they cover its origins, mechanism, and fundamental role.

accepted.label: ADALINE and MADALINE
accepted.description: Early adaptive linear neural networks (ADALINE, MADALINE) developed by Widrow and Hoff (1959) that used adaptive linear elements; MADALINE was the first neural network applied to a real-world problem (echo cancellation).
coverage_criteria: Explain what ADALINE and MADALINE stand for.
Identify echo cancellation as the first real-world application of a neural network (MADALINE).
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate provides sufficient detail.

accepted.label: Minsky & Papert critique and the AI winter
accepted.description: The 1969 book 'Perceptrons' by Minsky and Papert proved the limitations of single-layer perceptrons, leading to a halt in neural network funding and research throughout the 1970s.
coverage_criteria: Explain that Minsky and Papert demonstrated the inability of perceptrons to solve non-linearly separable problems (like XOR), causing a funding freeze.
Define the term 'AI winter' in the context of neural networks.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate captures the event.

accepted.label: Hopfield networks and the revival of neural network research
accepted.description: John Hopfield's 1982 paper and the US-Japan Conference on Cooperative Competitive Neural Networks rekindled interest and funding in neural networks, ending the AI winter.
coverage_criteria: State that Hopfield's 1982 approach and the US-Japan conference helped restart neural network funding.
Mention that the conference and the Japanese fifth-generation project spurred renewed investment.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate defines the revival.

accepted.label: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
accepted.description: A specialized recurrent neural network architecture using gated memory cells (forget, input, output gates) to learn long-term dependencies and mitigate the vanishing gradient problem; introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in 1997.
coverage_criteria: Explain the purpose of an LSTM: to handle long-term dependencies in sequences.
Name the three gates and their basic roles (forget, input, output).
Contrast LSTM with a simple RNN in terms of memory capability.
accepted.merge_rationale: c45 introduces LSTM historically, c46 provides architectural details, and c47 explains the gate types; together they form a complete lesson-local concept.

accepted.label: Backpropagation
accepted.description: The core learning algorithm for neural networks that computes the gradient of the loss function with respect to weights using the chain rule and updates weights in the opposite direction to minimize error.
coverage_criteria: List the four main steps of backpropagation: forward pass, loss computation, backward pass (gradient calculation), weight update.
Explain the role of the chain rule in propagating gradients from output to input layers.
accepted.merge_rationale: All candidates describe the backpropagation algorithm across different sources and languages; they reinforce the same teachable steps. The LeCun paper candidate (c45_pro_thinking_008) is pruned as an incidental application.

accepted.label: Feedforward neural network architecture
accepted.description: A neural network organized into sequential layers (input, hidden, output) where connections flow only forward without cycles; each neuron computes a weighted sum plus bias followed by an activation function.
coverage_criteria: Sketch a diagram of a feedforward network with at least one hidden layer.
Explain the function of weights and biases in a feedforward neuron.
accepted.merge_rationale: All candidates describe the layered, feedforward structure; c49 is the Portuguese-language equivalent.

accepted.label: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) basics
accepted.description: A neural network architecture with feedback connections that pass information from one time step to the next, creating an internal memory suitable for sequential data.
coverage_criteria: Explain how recurrent loops distinguish RNNs from feedforward networks.
Give an example of a task that benefits from recurrent architecture (e.g., language modeling, time series prediction).
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate defines the concept.

accepted.label: Autoencoder
accepted.description: An unsupervised neural network that compresses input into a lower-dimensional representation (encoding) and reconstructs the original input (decoding), useful for dimensionality reduction and feature learning.
coverage_criteria: Sketch the encoder-bottleneck-decoder structure.
Explain how an autoencoder can be used for data compression or denoising.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate provides the definition.

accepted.label: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
accepted.description: A framework where a generator network creates synthetic data and a discriminator network tries to distinguish it from real data; adversarial training improves both.
coverage_criteria: Explain the roles of the generator and discriminator.
Describe the adversarial training process as a two-player game.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate defines the concept.

accepted.label: Activation Functions
accepted.description: Non-linear activation functions (sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, step, softmax) applied to neuron outputs introduce non-linearity into the network, enabling learning of complex patterns. The sigmoid maps any real to (0,1); tanh to (-1,1); ReLU outputs max(0,x); step produces binary output.
coverage_criteria: List at least three activation functions with their formulas and typical output ranges.
Explain why non-linear activation functions are necessary in hidden layers.
Compare ReLU with sigmoid in terms of gradient flow and practical usage.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates describe various activation functions, their formulas, and their roles, together forming a single coherent teachable concept on activation functions.

accepted.label: Loss Functions
accepted.description: Loss functions quantify the prediction error during training, guiding weight updates. Mean squared error is used for regression, binary cross-entropy for classification; logistic loss is commonly used for binary classification.
coverage_criteria: Match loss functions (MSE, binary cross-entropy) to the appropriate problem type.
Write the logistic loss formula and explain its intuition.
accepted.merge_rationale: Both cover the purpose and specifics of loss functions, with one providing general types and the other focusing on logistic loss.

accepted.label: Convolutional Neural Networks
accepted.description: CNNs are architectures for grid-structured data (e.g., images) that use convolutional layers to detect spatial features, pooling layers to reduce dimensionality, and fully-connected layers for classification. Output size depends on input, filter, stride, and padding.
coverage_criteria: Describe the operation of a convolutional layer (filter, stride, feature map).
Compute the output size of a convolutional layer given input dimensions, filter size, and padding.
accepted.merge_rationale: c47_pro_thinking_006 adds practical output size computation to the CNN overview, completing the teachable concept.

accepted.label: Deep Residual Networks
accepted.description: Deep Residual Networks (DRNs) use skip connections (residual blocks) to allow gradients to flow through very deep architectures, mitigating the vanishing gradient problem and enabling training of networks like ResNet.
coverage_criteria: Explain what a residual block is and why it helps train very deep networks.
Name a well-known residual network architecture.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone concept on an advanced architecture.

accepted.label: Keras for Neural Networks
accepted.description: Keras is a high-level TensorFlow API that simplifies neural network construction. The Sequential model allows stacking layers; Dense layers are fully-connected; the input_shape argument specifies input dimensions; activation functions (e.g., ReLU) are set per layer.
coverage_criteria: Create a Keras Sequential model, add a Dense layer with a given number of neurons and activation, and specify input_shape.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates together cover the essential Keras API for building feedforward networks.

accepted.label: Overfitting and Regularization
accepted.description: Overfitting occurs when a model learns training noise and fails to generalize; underfitting is the opposite. Dropout is a regularization technique that randomly drops neurons during training to prevent overfitting.
coverage_criteria: Define overfitting and underfitting with examples.
Explain how dropout works and why it reduces overfitting.
accepted.merge_rationale: Dropout is a specific technique to combat overfitting, forming a unified concept with the general problem of overfitting.

accepted.label: Linear Algebra Foundations
accepted.description: Neural network computations rely on linear vector spaces, inner products, norms, and linear transformations. These concepts underpin weight matrices and forward/backward passes.
coverage_criteria: Define a linear vector space and list two axioms.
Compute the dot product of two vectors and explain its role in a neuron's weighted sum.
accepted.merge_rationale: Standalone mathematical prerequisite concept.

accepted.label: Gradient Descent Optimization
accepted.description: Gradient descent minimizes the loss by iteratively updating parameters: w = w - η * ∇J. The learning rate η controls step size; bias is an additional parameter; Adam adapts η per parameter; an epoch is one full pass over the dataset.
coverage_criteria: Write the gradient descent update rule for a weight.
Explain the role of the learning rate and describe the advantage of the Adam optimizer.
Define epoch and distinguish it from an iteration over a single sample.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates cover the core algorithm, hyperparameters (learning rate, bias), and training loop concepts, forming a comprehensive optimization concept.

accepted.label: Neural Network Training Implementation
accepted.description: Training involves: forward propagation to compute outputs; random weight initialization to break symmetry; a loop over epochs performing forward, cost, backward, and update steps; layer dimensions determine parameter shapes; caches store intermediate values for backprop.
coverage_criteria: List the steps in one training iteration (forward, cost, backward, update).
Explain why weights are initialized randomly and what happens if they are set to zero.
Describe the purpose of caching in forward propagation.
accepted.merge_rationale: These low-level implementation details together form a single coherent training procedure concept.

accepted.label: Perceptron and Its Limitations
accepted.description: The perceptron is a single neuron with step activation: output = step(∑ w_i x_i + b). Its training rule: w = w + η (d - y) x. It only solves linearly separable problems; XOR requires a hidden layer (e.g., two-layer network computing AND and OR).
coverage_criteria: Write the perceptron forward pass and training update rule.
Explain why a single perceptron cannot solve XOR and how a hidden layer enables the solution.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates explain the perceptron model, its training, the concept of linear separability, and the XOR limitation, with an explicit solution example.

accepted.label: Data Preparation for Neural Networks
accepted.description: Non-numeric inputs must be encoded (e.g., binary encoding, one-hot encoding) for neural networks. Datasets consist of features (attributes) and a target column, and data often needs to be numeric and normalized.
coverage_criteria: Choose an encoding scheme for a categorical variable (e.g., one-hot encoding) and justify.
Given a CSV, identify the feature columns and the target column.
accepted.merge_rationale: Both deal with preparing input data for neural networks, from encoding to dataset structure.

accepted.label: Divisão Treino/Teste
accepted.description: A técnica de separar dados em conjuntos de treino e teste para avaliar a generalização de modelos.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve escrever código para dividir um dataset em treino e teste.
O aluno deve explicar por que não se deve usar o mesmo conjunto para treino e teste.
accepted.merge_rationale: Candidato único representando o conceito de divisão treino/teste.

accepted.label: Implementação Manual vs Bibliotecas
accepted.description: Comparação entre implementar um perceptron do zero e usar scikit-learn, destacando a redução de código e complexidade.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve listar funções do scikit-learn usadas em substituição à implementação manual.
O aluno deve identificar vantagens e desvantagens de cada abordagem.
accepted.merge_rationale: Candidato único sobre a comparação de implementações.

accepted.label: Acurácia
accepted.description: Métrica de avaliação que calcula a proporção de predições corretas, variando de 0 a 1.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve calcular a acurácia a partir de predições e classes reais.
O aluno deve interpretar uma acurácia de 1.0 como separação perfeita para dados linearmente separáveis.
accepted.merge_rationale: Candidato único sobre a métrica de acurácia.

accepted.label: Perceptron Multicamadas
accepted.description: Introdução ao perceptron multicamadas como uma extensão para resolver problemas não-linearmente separáveis.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve diferenciar um perceptron simples de um multicamadas pela presença de camadas ocultas.
O aluno deve justificar a necessidade de camadas múltiplas para datasets não-lineares.
accepted.merge_rationale: Candidato único sobre perceptron multicamadas.
